title: the whole earth is one family
hookLine: where are you really from? a well-known line that starts with an insult
carry: for the generous heart, the earth is one family
tomorrow: Nani tells the Ramayana in English. is it still the Ramayana?

lines: BUT IT OPENS WITH AN INSULT.
cards: Where are you from? The kid names her town, the one with the soccer field and the bad pizza place. No, the grown-up says, kindly enough.
Where are you really from? An old Sanskrit line answers with a big idea: the whole earth is one family. But read the full verse and something odd turns up.
Before it says a word about family, it opens with an insult.

teach.h: MINE, A STRANGER: THE NARROW COUNT.
teach.b: The verse is in the Maha Upanishad, and in paraphrase it runs: this one is mine, that one is a stranger: that is how the narrow-hearted count. For those whose way of life is generous, the whole earth is one family.
In Sanskrit, the last words are vasudhaiva kutumbakam. Vasudha, the earth. Kutumbakam, a family, a household.
So why the insult first? Because the verse isn't making a claim about maps or bloodlines. It describes two ways of counting.
One sorts every face at a glance: mine, not mine. The other keeps a bigger household. And notice what it doesn't ask.
Nobody has to forget the town or the grandparents' village. Both can sit inside one household, because the household is the earth.
That's why where are you really from can sting: it assumes a person belongs to one place only. The verse counts more generously.
Many teachers read it through the Upanishads' biggest idea: the same atman, the same Self, lives in every being.
The Isha Upanishad says it plainly: whoever sees all beings in the Self, and the Self in all beings, shrinks from no one. Then the stranger was never really a stranger.
The puzzle, solved: the line about one family is the second half of a sentence about how small hearts do their math.

how: The line vasudhaiva kutumbakam is quoted by some Hindus, in India and abroad, as a picture of the generous heart: the whole earth as one family.

o: Hindu families with homes and roots in more than one land
Hindu pilgrims who travel each year to the holy rivers
Hindu monks who live outside India, without families

games.q: the generous count. tap the pairs.

s: the verse simply states that the earth is one family
it first calls 'this is mine, that one's a stranger' the narrow-hearted count.
kutumbakam means a family, a household
and vasudha is the earth: the whole earth as one household.
the verse asks people to give up their homeland
it widens the count. nobody has to forget a home.

games.q: at a family party, an uncle jokes that your best friend 'isn't one of us.' by the verse's count, what's the move?
o: laugh along. family means people who share your roots.
say nothing. the verse is about places, not people.
offer the bigger count: for the generous, the earth is one family.
games.why: the Maha Upanishad calls 'mine, a stranger' the narrow-hearted count. the generous count everyone in the household.

practice: Count on your fingers the places that have been home: a house, a street, a city, maybe one you only know from stories. Don't rank them. Fold each finger down as you go, until they're all held in one hand.

wordCard.voice: The diaspora: Hindu families with more than one home, and a verse that counts the whole earth as one household.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Maha Upanishad: the earth is a family. vasudha, the earth; kutumbakam, a household.
